questions.question: Nicolas Steno, a Danish anatomist in Florence, dissected the head of a great white shark in 1666 and saw that its teeth matched the 'tongue stones' found in rock. Where such a tooth lies sealed in rock, the rock carries the print of its every ridge and notch, but the tooth carries no print of the rock. What did Steno conclude from that?
questions.answer: The tooth was hard before the rock was
choices: The tooth was hard before the rock was
The rock was hard before the tooth was
The tooth and the rock hardened together
The tooth grew inside the hardened rock
questions.context: Of two solids, the one that hardened first leaves its print on the other, the way a boot leaves its print in wet mud, so the tooth was buried in soft sediment that only later hardened into rock. That led Steno to see rock layers as sediment settling one layer on another, the lowest first, which he set down in 1669 as the law of superposition. Many scholars before him held that such stones grew inside the rock by themselves.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the law of superposition and Nicolas Steno as the scientist who first stated it.

questions.question: William Smith, a canal surveyor and a blacksmith's son, studied the rock layers laid open by England's coal mines and canal cuts in the 1790s. Some layers looked much alike, a sandy layer here and a sandy layer there, yet Smith could tell each one from the rest and match it from place to place. What did he go by?
choices: The fossils in each layer
The thickness of each layer
The hardness of each layer
The depth of each layer
questions.context: Smith found that each layer holds fossils of its own, always in the same order, so a layer can be known by its fossils even where its rock looks like another's. Layers thin out, thicken and dip deeper from place to place, so their size and depth are poor guides. With his fossils Smith drew a map of the rocks of England and Wales in 1815, the first geological map of a whole country.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade Earth history teaches that fossils let geologists match rock layers from place to place, the method William Smith found.

questions.question: Geologists use index fossils to match rock layers from place to place and to tell which layers formed at the same time. Four kinds of ammonite, sea animals with coiled shells, left fossils behind. Which kind would make the best index fossil?
questions.answer: One that lived a short time all over the world
choices: One that lived a short time all over the world
One that lived a long time all over the world
One that lived a short time in one small bay
One that lived a long time in one small bay
questions.context: A fossil found all over the world can link layers on different continents, and one that lived for only a short time pins those layers to a narrow slice of the past. A kind that lived for a long time turns up in layers of many different ages, and one from a single bay links nothing far away. Ammonites and trilobites are classic index fossils.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches what makes a good index fossil (widespread, short-lived) when it teaches the relative dating of rock layers.

questions.question: James Hutton landed at Siccar Point, on the coast of Scotland, in 1788. Grey layers that once settled flat on a sea floor stand there almost on end, worn off across their tops, and layers of red sandstone lie over them. Geologists call such a junction an unconformity. What did Hutton conclude from it?
questions.answer: Earth's history reaches back an immense time
choices: Earth's history reaches back an immense time
One great flood laid down both kinds of rock
Both kinds of rock settled from one early ocean
Earth's rocks all formed in a few thousand years
questions.context: The grey layers had to settle, harden, be tipped on end and be worn flat before any red sand covered them, and Hutton knew how slowly such things happen today, so he reasoned the story needed an immense span of time. He wrote that he found 'no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end.' Many geologists of his day held instead that a great flood or one early ocean had laid down the rocks.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade accounts of Earth's history tell how Hutton's unconformity showed that Earth is vastly old.

questions.question: A geologist finds ripples set in stone across a layer of sandstone. They have the same shape as the ripples that flowing water makes on a sandy stream bed today, so she decides the sandstone formed from sand under flowing water. What is she assuming?
questions.answer: The same natural laws worked in the past as now
choices: The same natural laws worked in the past as now
The lowest layers are always the oldest ones
Each layer took the same time to form
Earth has always looked the way it does today
questions.context: She reads the old ripples by the rules that make ripples today, the assumption James Hutton built geology on, later called uniformitarianism. It does not mean Earth always looked the same: seas and mountains came and went, and rare great events happened, all under the same laws. The rule that lower layers are older is real, but she does not need it to read ripples.
questions.grade_note: The seventh-grade standard says science assumes nature's laws work in the past as they do today, and uses it to read rocks.

questions.question: Geologists of the 1800s built the geologic time scale, with its eras and periods, from the order of rock layers and the fossils in them. What could the layers and fossils alone not tell them?
questions.answer: How many years ago each period began
choices: How many years ago each period began
Which of two periods came first
Which kinds of life came before others
Which layers in two lands are the same age
questions.context: Layers and fossils give a relative age: which rock is older and which younger, and which layers far apart match. An absolute age is an age in years, and the time scale got its numbers only in the 1900s, from new ways of dating rocks. A wall of layers is like a stack of letters with no dates on them: the order shows, but not how long ago each was written.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches relative age (which is older) against absolute age (an age in years), and that layers and fossils give only the first.

questions.question: The geologic time scale divides Earth's history into eons, the longest spans, then eras, then periods. Its last three eras are the Paleozoic, the Mesozoic and the Cenozoic. What happened at the two lines between them?
questions.answer: Many kinds of living things died out together
choices: Many kinds of living things died out together
The first human beings appeared on Earth
A great ice age spread over the whole Earth
Rising seas covered all of Earth's land
questions.context: Both lines mark mass extinctions. The Paleozoic ended about 252 million years ago in the Great Dying, when about nine in ten kinds of sea life vanished, and the Mesozoic ended about 66 million years ago, when the last big dinosaurs died out with about three quarters of all species. Geologists drew the lines where the fossils change, and the first humans came only about 300,000 years ago.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that the time scale is divided at major changes in life, such as mass extinctions, read from the fossils in the layers.

questions.question: James Hutton saw 'no vestige of a beginning' in the rocks, and no one in his day could give Earth an age in years. Geologists now can, and the geologic time scale starts with Earth's birth. About how old is Earth?
choices: About 4.6 billion years
About 13.8 billion years
About 100 million years
About 4.6 million years
questions.context: Earth and the rest of the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago. About 13.8 billion years is the age of the whole universe, far older than Earth. In the 1800s Lord Kelvin, working from how fast Earth cools, gave it 20 to 400 million years, and John Phillips, from how fast mud piles up, about 96 million: both far too young.
questions.grade_note: The middle-school standard names Earth's 4.6-billion-year history as the span the geologic time scale organises.

questions.question: Squeeze all of Earth's history into a single day, from its birth at one midnight to the present at the next. On that clock the last of the big dinosaurs die out about twenty minutes before midnight. When do the first modern humans appear?
choices: A few seconds before midnight
A few minutes before midnight
About an hour before midnight
About noon, halfway through the day
questions.context: Each second of that day stands for about 53,000 years, so the 300,000 years since modern humans appeared fill only the last five or six seconds. The human family line splits from the chimpanzees' only about two minutes before midnight, and an hour before midnight the dinosaurs were still alive, so no person ever saw one. Many people picture humans and dinosaurs together, but some 66 million years lie between them.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade Earth history uses scale models of time, such as the one-day clock, to show how recently humans arrived.
